paragraphs.sourceText: “Don’t take many English courses; they won’t help you get a decent job. ” ‘‘ Sign up for management classes, so you’ll be ready to join the family business when you graduate. ”

paragraphs.sourceText: Sound 26 ? Many of us have heard suggestions like these 27 by parents or others close to us. Such comments often seem quite reasonable.
paragraphs.translationZh: 听起来很熟悉吗？我们中的许多人都听过父母或其他亲近的人提出的此类建议。这样的评论往往看起来很有道理。

paragraphs.sourceText: Why, then, should suggestions like these be taken with 28 ? The reason is they relate to decisions you should make. You are the one who must 29 their consequences.
paragraphs.translationZh: 那么，为什么要谨慎对待这些建议呢？原因是它们与您应该做出的决定有关。你是必须承担其后果的人。

paragraphs.sourceText: One of the worst reasons to follow a particular path in life is that other people want you to. Decisions that affect your life should be your decisions—decisions you make after you’ve considered various 30 and chosen the path that suits you best.
paragraphs.translationZh: 走某条人生道路的最糟糕的原因之一是其他人希望你这样做。影响你生活的决定应该是你自己的决定——你在考虑了各种选择并选择了最适合你的道路后做出的决定。

paragraphs.sourceText: Making your own decisions does not mean that you should 31 the suggestions of others. For instance, your parents do have their own unique experiences that may make their advice helpful, and having 32 in a great deal of your personal history, they may have a clear view of your strengths and weaknesses. Still, their views are not necessarily accurate. They may still see you as a child, 33 care and protection. Or they may see only your strengths. Or, in some unfortunate cases, they may 34 your flaws and shortcomings.
paragraphs.translationZh: 自己做出决定并不意味着您应该忽略他人的建议。例如，你的父母确实有自己独特的经历，这可能会让他们的建议很有帮助，并且在参与了你的大量个人经历后，他们可能对你的优点和缺点有清楚的了解。不过，他们的观点不一定准确。他们可能仍然将您视为需要照顾和保护的孩子。或者他们可能只看到你的优势。或者，在某些不幸的情况下，他们可能会关注你的缺点和缺点。

paragraphs.sourceText: People will always be giving you advice. Ultimately, though, you have to make your own 35 . .
paragraphs.translationZh: 人们总是会给你建议。但最终，你必须做出自己的判断。 。

paragraphs.sourceText: Questions 36 to 45 are based on the following passage.
paragraphs.translationZh: 第 36 至 45 题基于以下段落。

paragraphs.sourceText: One principle of taxation, called the benefits principle, states that people should pay taxes based on the benefits they receive from government services. This principle tries to make public goods similar to 36 goods. It seems reasonable that a person who often goes to the movies pays more in 37 for movie tickets than a person who rarely goes. And 38 , a person who gets great benefit from a public good should pay more for it than a person who gets little benefit.

The gasoline tax, for instance, is sometimes 39 using the benefits principle. In some states, 40 from the gasoline tax are used to build and maintain roads. Because those who buy gasoline are the same people who use the roads, the gasoline tax might be viewed as a 41 way to pay for this government service.

The benefits principle can also be used to argue that wealthy citizens should pay higher taxes than poorer ones, 42 because the wealthy benefit more from public services. Consider, for example, the benefits of police protection from 43 . Citizens with much to protect get greater benefit from police than those with less to protect. Therefore, according to the benefits principle, the wealthy should 44 more than the poor to the cost of 45 the police force. The same argument can be used for many other public services, such as fire protection, national defense, and the court system.

Directions ：In this section, you are going to read a passage with ten statements attached to it. Each statement contains information given in one of the paragraphs. Identify the paragraph from which the information is derived. You may choose a paragraph more than once. Each paragraph is marked with a letter. Answer the questions by marking the corresponding letter on Answer Sheet 2. Growing Up Colored
paragraphs.translationZh: 说明：在本节中，您将阅读一段附有十个陈述的段落。每条陈述都包含其中一个段落中给出的信息。确定信息来源的段落。您可以多次选择一个段落。每个段落都标有一个字母。通过在答题纸 2 上标记相应的字母来回答问题。成长有色人种

paragraphs.sourceText: A) You wouldn’t know Piedmont anymore—my Piedmont, I mean—the town in West Virginia where I learned to be a colored boy.
paragraphs.translationZh: 答）你不会再了解皮埃蒙特了——我的意思是——西弗吉尼亚州的那个小镇，我在那里学会了成为一个黑人男孩。

paragraphs.sourceText: B) The 1950s in Piedmont was a time to remember, or at least to me. People were always proud to be from Piedmont—lying at the foot of a mountain, on the banks of the mighty Potomac. We knew God gave America no more beautiful location. I never knew colored people anywhere who were crazier about mountains and water, flowers and trees, fishing and hunting. For as long as anyone could remember, we could outhunt, outshoot, and outswim the white boys in the valley.
paragraphs.translationZh: B) 20 世纪 50 年代的皮埃蒙特是一个值得铭记的时代，至少对我来说是这样。人们总是为自己来自皮埃蒙特而感到自豪——位于山脚下、波托马克河畔。我们知道上帝没有给美国提供比这更美丽的地方。我从未见过比任何地方的有色人种更疯狂地热爱山水、花草树木、钓鱼和狩猎的人。从人们记事起，我们就可以在山谷里追捕、射击和游泳上战胜白人男孩。

paragraphs.sourceText: C) The social structure of Piedmont was something we knew like the back of our hands. It was an immigrant town; white Piedmont was Italian and Irish, with a handful of wealthy WASPs (益格鲁撒克逊裔的白人新教徒）on East Hampshire Street, and “ethnic” neighborhoods of working-class people everywhere else, colored and white.
paragraphs.translationZh: C) 皮埃蒙特的社会结构我们了如指掌。这是一个移民小镇；皮埃蒙特白人是意大利人和爱尔兰人，东汉普郡街上有少数富有的黄蜂族（益格鲁撒克逊裔的白人新移民），其他地方也有工人阶级的“民族”社区，有色人种和白人。

paragraphs.sourceText: D) For as long as anyone can remember, Piedmonts character has been completely bound up with the Westvaco paper mill: its prosperous past and doubtful future. At first glance, the town is a typical dying mill center. Many once beautiful buildings stand empty, evidencing a bygone time of spirit and pride. The big houses on East Hampshire Street are no longer proud, as they were when I was a kid.
paragraphs.translationZh: D) 从人们记事起，皮埃蒙特的特色就一直与 Westvaco 造纸厂紧密相连：它繁荣的过去和令人怀疑的未来。乍一看，这个小镇是一个典型的染色工厂中心。许多曾经美丽的建筑如今已空无一人，见证着过去的精神和自豪时光。东汉普郡街上的大房子不再像我小时候那样骄傲。

paragraphs.sourceText: E) Like the Italians and the Irish, most of the colored people migrated to Piedmont at the turn of the 20th century to work at the paper mill, which opened in 1888. All the colored men at the paper mill worked on “the platform” —loading paper into trucks until the craft unions were finally integrated in 1968. Loading is what Daddy did every working day of his life. That’s what almost every colored grown-up I knew did.
paragraphs.translationZh: E) 与意大利人和爱尔兰人一样，大多数有色人种在 20 世纪之交迁移到皮埃蒙特，在 1888 年开业的造纸厂工作。造纸厂的所有有色人种都在“平台”上工作——将纸张装进卡车，直到 1968 年工会最终合并。装货是爸爸一生中每个工作日所做的事情。我认识的几乎所有有色人种成年人都是这么做的。

paragraphs.sourceText: F) Colored people lived in three neighborhoods that were clearly separated. Welcome to the Colored Zone, a large stretched banner could have said. And it felt good in there, like walking around your house in bare feet and underwear, or snoring (打鼾) right out loud on the couch in front of the TV—enveloped by the comforts of home, the warmth of those you love.
paragraphs.translationZh: F) 有色人种居住在三个明显分开的社区中。欢迎来到彩色区，一条巨大的拉长横幅可以这样写。在那里感觉很好，就像光着脚和内衣在家里走来走去，或者在电视机前的沙发上大声打鼾——被家的舒适和你所爱的人的温暖所包围。

paragraphs.sourceText: G) Of course, the colored world was not so much a neighborhood as a condition of existence. And though our own world was seemingly self-contained, it impacted on the white world of Piedmont in almost every direction. Certainly, the borders of our world seemed to be impacted on when some white man or woman showed up where he or she did not belong, such as at the black Legion Hall. Our space was violated when one of them showed up at a dance or a party. The rhythms would be off. The music would sound not quite right. Everybody would leave early.
paragraphs.translationZh: G) 当然，有色世界与其说是一个社区，不如说是一种存在条件。尽管我们自己的世界看似独立，但它几乎从各个方向影响着皮埃蒙特的白人世界。当然，当一些白人男性或女性出现在他或她不属于的地方（例如黑人军团大厅）时，我们世界的边界似乎会受到影响。当他们中的一个出现在舞会或聚会上时，我们的空间就被侵犯了。节奏就会被打乱。音乐听起来不太对劲。大家都会早点离开。

paragraphs.sourceText: H) Before 1955, most white people were just shadowy presences in our world, vague figures of power like remote bosses at the mill or clerks at the bank. There were exceptions, of course, the white people who would come into our world in routine, everyday ways we all understood. Mr. Mail Man, Mr. Insurance Man, Mr. White-and-Chocolate Milk Man, Mr. Landlord Man, Mr. Police Man ：we called white people by their trade, like characters in a mystery play. Mr. Insurance Man would come by every other week to collect payments on college or death policies, sometimes 50 cents or less.
paragraphs.translationZh: H) 1955 年之前，大多数白人只是我们世界中的影子，是模糊的权力人物，就像工厂的远程老板或银行的职员。当然，也有例外，白人会以我们都理解的日常方式进入我们的世界。邮件人先生、保险人先生、白巧克力牛奶人先生、房东人先生、警察人先生：我们按职业来称呼白人，就像推理剧中的人物一样。保险人先生每隔一周就会过来收取大学保单或死亡保单的付款，有时是 50 美分或更少。

paragraphs.sourceText: I) “It’s no disgrace to be colored, ” the black entertainer Bert Williams famously observed early in the century, “but it is awfully inconvenient.” For most of my childhood, we couldn’t eat in restaurants or sleep in hotels, we couldn’t use certain bathrooms or try on clothes in stores. Mama insisted that we dress up when we went to shop. She was carefully dressed when she went to clothing stores, and wore white pads called shields under her arms so her dress or blouse would show no sweat. “We’d like to try this on,” she’d say carefully, uttering her words precisely and properly. “We don’t buy clothes we can’t try on, she’d say when they declined, and we^ walk out in Mama’s dignified (有尊严的）manner. She preferred to shop where we h ad an account and where everyone knew who she was.
paragraphs.translationZh: I) “有色人种并不是什么耻辱，”黑人艺人伯特·威廉姆斯 (Bert Williams) 在本世纪初曾说过一句名言，“但它非常不方便。”在我童年的大部分时间里，我们不能在餐馆吃饭或在酒店睡觉，我们不能使用某些浴室或在商店试穿衣服。妈妈坚持要求我们去商店时盛装打扮。当她去服装店时，她会精心打扮，腋下夹着白色的垫子，称为盾牌，这样她的衣服或衬衫就不会流汗。 “我们想试穿一下，”她小心翼翼地说，语气准确、得体。 “我们不会买不能试穿的衣服，当他们拒绝时，她会说，然后我们以妈妈有尊严的方式走出去。她更喜欢在我们有账户、每个人都知道她是谁的地方购物。

paragraphs.sourceText: J) At the Cut-Rate Drug Store, no one colored was allowed to sit down at the counter or tables, with one exception：my father. I don5t know for certain why Carl Dadisman, the owner, wouldn’t stop Daddy from sitting down. But I believe it was in part because Daddy was so light-colored, and in part because, during his shift at the phone company, he picked up orders for food and coffee for the operators. Colored people were supposed to stand at the counter, get their food to go, and leave. Even when Young Doc Bess would set up the basketball team with free Cokes after one of many victories, the colored players had to stand around and drink out of paper cups while the white players and cheerleaders sat down in comfortable chairs and drank out of glasses.
paragraphs.translationZh: J) 在减价药店，任何有色人种都不允许坐在柜台或桌子旁，只有一个例外：我的父亲。我不确定为什么店主卡尔·达迪斯曼不阻止爸爸坐下。但我相信这部分是因为爸爸的肤色太浅，部分是因为他在电话公司值班期间，为接线员接了食物和咖啡的订单。有色人种应该站在柜台前，拿走食物，然后离开。即使年轻的贝斯医生在一场胜利后为篮球队提供免费的可乐，黑人球员也必须站着用纸杯喝水，而白人球员和拉拉队队员则坐在舒适的椅子上用玻璃杯喝水。

paragraphs.sourceText: K) I couldn’t have been much older than five or six as I sat with my father at the Cut-Rate one afternoon, enjoying ice cream. Mr. Wilson, a stony-faced Irishman, walked by. “Hello, Mr. Wilson, ”my father said. “Hello, George.”
paragraphs.translationZh: K) 一天下午，当我和父亲坐在 Cut-Rate 餐厅享用冰淇淋时，我的年龄不可能超过五六岁。威尔逊先生是一位面无表情的爱尔兰人，从他身边走过。 “你好，威尔逊先生，”我父亲说。 “你好，乔治。”

paragraphs.sourceText: L) I was genuinely puzzled. Mr. Wilson must have confused my father with somebody else, but who? There weren’t any Georges among the colored people in Piedmont. ‘‘Why don’t you tell him your name, Daddy?” I asked loudly. “Your name isn’t George.” “He knows my name, boy，” my father said after a long pause. “He calls all colored people George. ”
paragraphs.translationZh: L) 我真的很困惑。威尔逊先生肯定把我父亲和其他人搞混了，但是谁呢？皮埃蒙特的有色人种中没有乔治。 “爸爸，你为什么不告诉他你的名字呢？”我大声问道。 “你的名字不是乔治。” “他知道我的名字，孩子，”我父亲停顿了很长时间后说道。 “他称所有有色人种为乔治。 ”

paragraphs.sourceText: M) I knew we wouldn’t talk about it again; even at that age, I was given to understand that there were some subjects it didn’t do to worry to death about. Now that I have children, I realize that what distressed my father wasn’t so much the Mr. Wilsons of the world as the painful obligation to explain the racial facts of life to someone who hadn’t quite learned them yet. Maybe Mr. Wilson couldn’t hurt my father by calling him George; but I hurt him by asking to know why.
paragraphs.translationZh: M) 我知道我们不会再谈论这件事了；即使在那个年纪，我也明白有些事情是不需要担心得要死的。现在我有了孩子，我意识到让我父亲痛苦的并不是世界上的威尔逊先生，而是向一个还没有完全了解生活中的种族事实的人解释痛苦的义务。也许威尔逊先生称呼我父亲为乔治不会伤害他；也许威尔逊先生叫他乔治不会伤害他。但我问他为什么伤害了他。

paragraphs.sourceText: 46. The author felt as a boy that his life in a separated neighborhood was casual and cozy.
paragraphs.translationZh: 46. 提交人觉得，作为一个男孩，他在隔离社区的生活是随意而舒适的。

paragraphs.sourceText: 47. There is every sign of decline at the paper mill now.
paragraphs.translationZh: 47. 造纸厂现在有各种衰落的迹象。

paragraphs.sourceText: 48. One reason the author’s father could sit and eat at the drug store was that he didn’t look that dark.
paragraphs.translationZh: 48. 提交人的父亲能够坐在药店吃饭的原因之一是他看起来没那么黑。

paragraphs.sourceText: 49. Piedmont was a town of immigrants from different parts of the world.
paragraphs.translationZh: 49. 皮埃蒙特是一个来自世界各地的移民的城镇。

paragraphs.sourceText: 50. In spite of the awful inconveniences caused by racial prejudice, the author’s family managed to live a life of dignity.
paragraphs.translationZh: 50. 尽管种族偏见造成了极大的不便，提交人的家人还是过上了有尊严的生活。

paragraphs.sourceText: 51. The author later realized he had caused great distress to his father by asking why he was wrongly addressed.
paragraphs.translationZh: 51. 提交人后来认识到，他询问为何对他的称呼是错误的，这给他父亲带来了极大的痛苦。

paragraphs.sourceText: 52. The author took pride in being from Piedmont because of its natural beauty.
paragraphs.translationZh: 52. 作者因来自皮埃蒙特而感到自豪，因为这里的自然美景。

paragraphs.sourceText: 53. Colored people called white people by the business they did.
paragraphs.translationZh: 53.有色人种根据他们所做的事情来称呼白人。

paragraphs.sourceText: 54. Colored people who lived in Piedmont did heavy manual jobs at the paper mill.
paragraphs.translationZh: 54. 居住在皮埃蒙特的有色人种在造纸厂从事繁重的体力劳动。

paragraphs.sourceText: 55. The colored people felt uneasy at the presence of the whites in their neighborhoods.
paragraphs.translationZh: 55. 有色人种对白人出现在他们的社区感到不安。

paragraphs.sourceText: Directions：There are 2 passages in this section. Each passage is followed by some questions or unfinished statements. For each of them there are four choices marked A) 9 B), C) and D). You should decide on the best choice and mark the corresponding letter on Answer Sheet 2 with a single line through the centre.
paragraphs.translationZh: 说明：本节有2个段落。每段文章后面都有一些问题或未完成的陈述。每个选项都有四个选项，标记为 A) 9 B)、C) 和 D)。您应该决定最佳选择，并在答题卡 2 上用一条穿过中心的单线标记相应的字母。

paragraphs.sourceText: Questions 56 to 60 are based on the following passage.
paragraphs.translationZh: 第 56 至 60 题基于以下段落。

paragraphs.sourceText: Children are a delight. They are our future. But sadly, hiring someone to take care of them while you go to work is getting more expensive by the year.
paragraphs.translationZh: 孩子们是一种享受。他们是我们的未来。但遗憾的是，在你上班时雇人照顾他们的费用逐年上涨。

paragraphs.sourceText: Earlier this month，it was reported that the cost of enrolling an infant or small kid at a childcare center rose 3% in 2012, faster than the overall cost of living. There are now large strips of the country where daycare for an infant costs more than a tenth of the average married coupled income.
paragraphs.translationZh: 本月早些时候，有报道称，2012 年，婴儿或小孩在托儿中心的入学费用上涨了 3%，涨幅超过了总体生活成本。现在，该国大部分地区的婴儿日托费用超过已婚夫妇平均收入的十分之一。

paragraphs.sourceText: This is not necessarily a new trend, but it is a somewhat puzzling one. The price of professional childcare has been rising since the 1980s. Yet during that time, pay for professional childcare workers has stood still. Actually caregivers make less today, in real terms, than they did in 1990. Considering that labor costs are responsible for up to 80% of a daycare centers expenses, one would expect flat wages to have meant flat prices.
paragraphs.translationZh: 这不一定是一种新趋势，但却是一个有点令人费解的趋势。自 20 世纪 80 年代以来，专业托儿服务的价格一直在上涨。然而在此期间，专业儿童保育人员的工资却停滞不前。事实上，按实际价值计算，今天看护者的收入比 1990 年要少。考虑到劳动力成本占日托中心费用的 80%，人们会认为工资不变就意味着价格不变。

paragraphs.sourceText: So who^ to blame for higher childcare costs? Childcare is a carefully regulated industry. States lay down rules about how many children each employee is allowed to watch over, the space care centers need per child, and other minute details. And the stricter the regulations, the higher the costs. If it has to hire a caregiver for every two children, it can^ really achieve any economies of scale on labor to save money when other expenses go up. In Massachusetts, where childcare centers must hire one teacher for every three infants, the price of care averaged more than $ 16,000 per year. In Mississippi, where centers must hire one teacher for every five infants, the price of care averaged less than $ 5,000.
paragraphs.translationZh: 那么谁应该为更高的托儿费用负责呢？儿童保育是一个受到严格监管的行业。各州制定了规定，规定每个员工可以照顾多少个孩子、空间护理中心需要每个孩子以及其他细节。而且监管越严格，成本就越高。如果它必须为每两个孩子雇用一名保姆，那么它就可以真正实现劳动力规模经济，以便在其他费用增加时节省开支。在马萨诸塞州，儿童保育中心必须为每三个婴儿雇用一名教师，平均每年的保育费用超过 16,000 美元。在密西西比州，中心必须为每五个婴儿雇用一名教师，平均护理价格不到 5,000 美元。

paragraphs.sourceText: Unfortunately, I don^ have all the daycare-center regulations handy. But I wouldn’t be surprised if as the rules have become more elaborate, prices have risen. The tradeoff (交换) might be worth it in some cases; after all，the health and safety of children should probably come before cheap service. But certainly, it doesn’t seem to be an accident that some of the cheapest daycare available is in the least regulated South.
paragraphs.translationZh: 不幸的是，我手边没有所有日托中心的规定。但如果随着规则变得更加复杂，价格上涨，我也不会感到惊讶。在某些情况下，这种权衡可能是值得的；毕竟，儿童的健康和安全可能应该优先于廉价服务。但当然，一些最便宜的日托中心位于监管最少的南方似乎并非偶然。

paragraphs.sourceText: Questions 61 to 65 are based on the following passage.
paragraphs.translationZh: 第 61 至 65 题基于以下段落。

paragraphs.sourceText: Alex Pang’s amusing new book The Distraction Addiction addresses those of us who feel panic without a cellphone or computer. And that, he claims, is pretty much all of us. When we’re not online, where we spend four months annually, we’re engaged in the stressful work of trying to get online.
paragraphs.translationZh: 亚历克斯·彭（Alex Pang）有趣的新书《分心成瘾》针对的是我们这些在没有手机或电脑的情况下感到恐慌的人。他声称，这几乎就是我们所有人的情况。当我们每年有四个月不上网时，我们就会从事上网的压力很大的工作。

paragraphs.sourceText: The Distraction Addiction is not framed as a self-help book. It’s a thoughtful examination of the dangers of our computing overdose and a historical overview of how technological advances change consciousness. A “professional futurist”, Pang urges an approach which he calls “contemplative (沉思的）computing. ” He asks that you pay full attention to “ how your mind and body interact with computers and how your attention and creativity are influenced by technology.”
paragraphs.translationZh: 《分心成瘾》并不是一本自助书。这是对我们过度使用计算的危险进行的深思熟虑的审视，也是对技术进步如何改变意识的历史概述。作为一名“专业未来学家”，庞提倡一种他称之为“沉思的计算”的方法。他要求你充分关注“你的思想和身体如何与计算机互动，以及你的注意力和创造力如何受到技术的影响”。

paragraphs.sourceText: Pang’s first job is to free you from the common misconception that doing two things at once allows you to get more done. What is commonly called multitasking is, in fact, switch-tasking, and its harmful effects on productivity are well documented. Pang doesn’t advocate returning to a pre-Internet world. Instead, he asks you to “take a more ecological(生态的)view of your relationships with technologies and look for ways devices or media may be making specific tasks easier or faster but at the same time making your work and life harder.
paragraphs.translationZh: 庞的第一份工作就是让你摆脱一种常见的误解，即同时做两件事可以让你完成更多工作。通常所说的多任务处理实际上是任务切换，它对生产力的有害影响是有据可查的。庞并不主张回到互联网出现之前的世界。相反，他要求你“以更生态的方式看待你与技术的关系，并寻找设备或媒体可能使特定任务变得更容易或更快，但同时使你的工作和生活变得更加困难的方式。

paragraphs.sourceText: The Distraction Addiction is particularly fascinating on how technologies have changed certain fields of labor—often for the worse. For architects, computer-aided design has become essential but in some ways has cheapened the design process. As one architect puts it, “Architecture is first and foremost about thinking... and drawing is a more productive way of thinking” than computer-aided design. Somewhat less amusing are Pang’s solutions for kicking the Internet habit. He recommends the usual behavior-modification approaches, familiar to anyone who has completed a quit-smoking program. Keep logs to study your online profile and decide what you can knock out, download a program like Freedom that locks you out of your browser, or take a “digital Sabbath（安息日）”. “Unless you’re a reporter or emergency-department doctor, you^ discover that your world doesn’t fall apart when you go offline.
paragraphs.translationZh: 《分心成瘾》特别引人入胜的是技术如何改变某些劳动领域——通常是变得更糟。对于建筑师来说，计算机辅助设计已经变得至关重要，但在某些方面降低了设计过程的成本。正如一位建筑师所说，“建筑首先是关于思考……而绘图是一种比计算机辅助设计更高效的思维方式”。庞的戒除上网习惯的解决方案就没那么有趣了。他推荐了通常的行为改变方法，任何完成戒烟计划的人都熟悉这些方法。保存日志以研究您的在线个人资料并决定您可以删除什么，下载像 Freedom 这样将您锁定在浏览器之外的程序，或者参加“数字安息日”。 “除非你是一名记者或急诊室医生，否则你会发现当你离线时你的世界并没有崩溃。
